name: Adam (Jingjing)
otherNames: King-Tsing (A. Wylie's English of the stele)
knownFor: The priest who composed the Chinese text of the Xi'an stele, set up in 781. The text sets out the faith of the Church of the East and tells its story in Tang China.
dates: The stele was set up in 781, by A. Wylie's English of its Chinese date. No source used here gives his birth or death
place: Tang China. No source used here says where he came from
tradition: The Church of the East on the Silk Road
role: Priest; author of the Chinese text of the Xi'an stele

keyWorks.title: The Chinese text of the Xi'an stele
keyWorks.about: a preface and an ode. It sets out God, the cross, the Messiah, baptism and the church's ways, then tells of Alopen and the emperors who favored the church. Held in A. Wylie's English

traces: His text is the main source for Alopen and the coming of the Church of the East to China.
In his text the church names itself the Illustrious Religion.
remembered: Henry Yule reads the Syriac on the stone as naming Adam, "Bishop and Pope" of China.
T. J. Lamy, as J.-B. Chabot quotes him, writes that Adam was bishop of China when the stone was engraved.

uncertain: Everything the sources used here say of him comes from the stone, apart from one note of Henri Cordier's. No source used here gives his birth, his death or where he came from.
That King-Tsing is Adam. The Chinese names its author King-Tsing; the Syriac names Adam. Cordier, in his notes to Yule, joins the two names.

His rank. Assemani reads the Syriac as priest, chorepiscopus and papas of China. Kircher's English in Malech has "Deacon, Vicar-episcopal and Pope". Assemani calls the deacon a misreading. Yule has bishop.
Who set up the stone. The Syriac, in Assemani's Latin and in Kircher's English, says the priest Jazedbuzid set it up. Cordier says Adam erected it.

A Buddhist sutra. Cordier writes that it appears King-tsing also helped a Buddhist translate a sutra, the Satparamita, from a Hu text. He cites a paper by J. Takakusu, which is not among the sources used here.
Two Adams. The stone also names Adam the deacon, a son of Jazedbuzid. He is a different man.
The Chinese text. It is not legible in any held file, so his words are read in Wylie's English.
